title: The periodic table and periodic trends
blurb: Read periods, groups, shells and valence electrons from the table, name the main families and predict radius, ionization energy, electronegativity and reactivity from position.
question: Phosphorus has atomic number 15 and chlorine has 17. Without a periodic table, how many shells and valence electrons does each have, and which one has the smaller atoms and the stronger pull on electrons?

teach.body: Formally, the modern periodic table lists elements by increasing atomic number (Moseley); Mendeleev's first table used atomic mass. Periods are the 7 rows: the period number equals the number of occupied electron shells. Groups (families) are the 18 columns: members share the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike. In plain English: the row tells you how big the atom's 'house' is; the column tells you how it acts.

head: Element (Z)
Shells
Period
Valence e⁻
teach.caption: Shells fill from the inside: 2, then 8, then 8, then 2 for the first 20 elements (capacity 2n²: 2, 8, 18). The last number is the valence count.

teach.h: Valence electrons and the octet rule
teach.body: Valence electrons sit in the outermost shell and decide bonding. Main groups: group 1 has 1, group 2 has 2, and groups 13 to 18 have the group number minus 10 (group 16 has 6; helium has 2). Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 (the octet rule). So group 1 forms +1 ions, group 2 +2, aluminum +3, group 15 −3, group 16 −2 and group 17 −1; noble gases form essentially none.

head: Group
Family
Key facts
rows: 1 valence e⁻; +1 ions; most reactive metals (not H)
Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au; variable charges
7 valence e⁻; −1 ions; most reactive nonmetals
teach.caption: Metals sit left and center, nonmetals upper right (plus hydrogen), metalloids such as Si and Ge along the staircase. Hg and Br are the liquid elements.

teach.body: Across a period, each element adds a proton while the electrons stay in the same number of shells. The stronger pull draws the shells in: atoms get smaller, harder to strip (higher ionization energy) and greedier for shared electrons (higher electronegativity). Down a group, each element adds a whole shell. Outer electrons sit farther out, so atoms get larger and hold them less tightly.

teach.caption: Fluorine (top right) is the most electronegative element; cesium and francium (bottom left) are the most reactive metals. Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger.
Radius shrinks left to right while ionization energy and electronegativity climb: Na < Mg < S < Cl in electronegativity.

teach.body: Marcus, an LPN applicant, fills phosphorus's 15 electrons: 2, 8, 5. Three shells means period 3; five valence electrons means group 15. It sits upper right, so it is a nonmetal that gains 3 electrons to reach an octet (P³⁻). Chlorine (2, 8, 7) is in the same period but two places right: more protons on the same three shells, so chlorine is smaller and more electronegative.

teach.text: Groups (columns) share properties; periods (rows) share only the number of shells. Radius DECREASES left to right even though atoms get heavier. Electronegativity peaks at the TOP RIGHT (fluorine). For groups 13 to 18, subtract 10: group 16 has 6 valence electrons, not 16. And hydrogen sits in group 1 but is a nonmetal.

items: Ordered by atomic number. Period number = occupied shells; group = valence electrons for main groups.
Shells fill 2, 8, 8, 2 for the first 20 elements; atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach an octet.
Group 1 alkali metals and group 17 halogens are the most reactive families; group 18 noble gases are inert.
Across a period: radius down; ionization energy and electronegativity up. Down a group: the reverse.
Fluorine is the most electronegative; cesium and francium are the most reactive metals.

summary: You can now use an element's shells and valence electrons to find its period and group, predict its usual ion and name its family. You can also predict how atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity and metallic character change across a period and down a group.

A.q: Calcium has atomic number 20. What is the electron arrangement of a neutral calcium atom, by shell?
A.why: Fill from the inside: 2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, 8 in shell 3, then the last 2 in shell 4: 2, 8, 8, 2.

whyNot.0: For the first 20 elements, shell 3 takes 8 before shell 4 starts.
whyNot.2: The inner shells fill first; shell 2 holds 8 before any electrons enter shell 3.
whyNot.3: Shell 2 holds a maximum of 8, so it cannot hold 18.

A.q: Moving from left to right across period 3, what happens to atomic radius?
A.why: Each step adds a proton but no new shell, so the stronger pull draws the electrons closer and the atoms shrink.

whyNot.0: Radius increases DOWN a group (new shells), not across a period.
whyNot.1: The shell count stays the same, but the rising nuclear charge does shrink the atoms.
whyNot.2: There is no rise-then-fall pattern; the radius shrinks across the period.

A.q: Which group contains the most reactive nonmetals?
A.why: The halogens (group 17) have 7 valence electrons and need just one more, making them the most reactive nonmetals.

whyNot.0: Alkali metals are the most reactive METALS, not nonmetals.
whyNot.2: Noble gases have a full outer shell and are very unreactive.
whyNot.3: Alkaline earth metals are metals that form +2 ions.

B.q: Sulfur is in group 16 of the periodic table. Which ion does sulfur most commonly form?
B.why: Group 16 elements have 6 valence electrons. Gaining 2 completes the octet, giving S²⁻ (sulfide).

whyNot.0: Losing 6 electrons takes far more energy than gaining 2; nonmetals gain electrons.
whyNot.1: A 2+ charge means losing electrons; sulfur gains 2 to reach 8.
whyNot.3: Gaining 6 would give 12 valence electrons, past the octet.

B.why: Potassium is below sodium in group 1; its valence electron is farther out and lost more easily, so it reacts more vigorously.

whyNot.0: Ionization energy decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower.
whyNot.1: Potassium has an extra shell, so its radius is larger.
whyNot.2: Electronegativity decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower.

B.q: An element's atoms have the arrangement 2, 8, 6. In which period and group is it?
B.why: Three occupied shells means period 3. Six valence electrons in a main group means group 16 (6 + 10). The element is sulfur.

whyNot.1: The period is the number of shells (3), not the valence count.
whyNot.2: In groups 13 to 18 the valence count is the group number minus 10, so 6 valence electrons is group 16.
whyNot.3: Electrons fill three shells, so the element is in period 3, not period 2.

C.q: Which list places these elements in order of INCREASING first ionization energy?
C.why: All three are in period 3. Ionization energy rises left to right: Na (group 1) < Mg (group 2) < Cl (group 17).

whyNot.0: This is decreasing order: chlorine, on the right, has the highest ionization energy.
whyNot.2: Magnesium is to the right of sodium, so its ionization energy is higher, not lower.
whyNot.3: Chlorine is farthest right, so it belongs last (highest), after magnesium.

C.q: In a demonstration, lithium fizzes steadily in water and sodium darts around rapidly. What should the class predict for potassium?
options: Slower, because it has more protons
Slower, because its ionization energy is higher
Faster, because its outer electron is farther out
About the same, because all have one valence electron
C.why: Down group 1 the valence electron sits in a higher shell, farther from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily and the reaction is more vigorous.

whyNot.0: More protons are outweighed by the extra shell; reactivity of metals increases down a group.
whyNot.1: Ionization energy decreases down a group, so potassium's is lower, not higher.
whyNot.3: Sharing one valence electron explains why they react alike, but reactivity still rises down the group.

C.q: Element X is in group 2 and element Y is in group 17 of the same period. Which statement is correct?
options: X is larger and forms X²⁺ ions
X is smaller and forms X²⁻ ions
Y is larger and forms Y⁺ ions
Y is smaller and forms Y⁷⁻ ions
C.why: X is farther left in the period, so it has fewer protons pulling the same shells: larger. With 2 valence electrons it loses them to form X²⁺.

whyNot.1: Atoms farther left are larger, and group 2 metals lose electrons to form 2+ ions.
whyNot.2: Y is smaller (more protons, same shells) and, with 7 valence electrons, gains 1 to form Y⁻.
whyNot.3: Y is smaller, but it gains just 1 electron to complete its octet, forming Y⁻.

reteach.title: Magnets and distance
reteach.question: Hold a paperclip near a magnet, then farther away, then near a stronger magnet. How does that explain every periodic trend?

blocks.body: The nucleus is a magnet and the outer electrons are paperclips. Going across a period turns up the magnet's strength (more protons) while the paperclips stay the same distance away (same shells): they are pulled in tighter, so atoms shrink and grip harder. Going down a group moves the paperclips farther away (new shells): the grip weakens, atoms swell and lose electrons more easily.

blocks.h: Turn a dial, see the effect

blocks.text: Heavier does not mean bigger. Chlorine has more mass than sodium, yet its atoms are smaller because its stronger nucleus pulls the same three shells closer.

explain.body: The period number is the number of occupied shells. Main-group elements in the same group share their number of valence electrons, so they share chemical properties. Shells fill 2, 8, 8, 2 for the first 20 elements.

test.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium react with water in similar ways. What do their atoms have in common?
test.why: All three are in group 1, so each has one valence electron, and valence electrons decide chemical behavior.

whyNot.0: They have 2, 3 and 4 shells; elements in the same period share shell counts.
whyNot.2: A full outer shell describes the unreactive noble gases.
whyNot.3: Radius increases down the group as shells are added.

explain.body: Groups 1 and 2 have 1 and 2 valence electrons; groups 13 to 18 have the group number minus 10. Atoms move toward an octet: metals lose electrons (cations), nonmetals gain them (anions).

test.q: Nitrogen is in group 15. How many valence electrons does it have, and which ion does it tend to form?
test.why: Group 15 minus 10 = 5 valence electrons. Gaining 3 reaches an octet, giving N³⁻.

whyNot.0: The ion is right, but group 15 elements have 5 valence electrons, not 15: subtract 10 for groups 13 to 18.
whyNot.2: Losing 5 electrons takes far more energy than gaining 3; nonmetals gain electrons.
whyNot.3: 3 is the number of electrons nitrogen gains, not its valence count, and gaining gives a negative ion.

explain.body: Group 1 alkali metals (most reactive metals), group 2 alkaline earth metals, groups 3 to 12 transition metals, group 17 halogens (most reactive nonmetals) and group 18 noble gases (full shell, inert).

test.q: An element is a colorless gas whose atoms have a full outer shell and almost never form compounds. Which group is it in?
test.why: A full outer shell and almost no reactivity describe the noble gases, group 18.

whyNot.0: Group 1 alkali metals are highly reactive solids with one valence electron.
whyNot.1: Group 2 alkaline earth metals are reactive metals that form +2 ions.
whyNot.2: Halogens are one electron short of a full shell, making them highly reactive.

explain.body: Across a period: radius falls; ionization energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group: radius rises; ionization energy and electronegativity fall; metals become more reactive.

test.q: Electronegativity increases across a period mainly because:
options: more protons pull on the same shells
the atoms lose their valence electrons
test.why: Across a period the nuclear charge rises while electrons stay in the same shells, so the atom pulls shared electrons harder.

whyNot.0: The shell count stays the same across a period; it rises down a group.
whyNot.2: Atoms on the right tend to gain electrons, not lose them.
whyNot.3: Neutrons carry no charge and do not explain the trend; the rising proton count does.
